title: How to Read a Government Solicitation
description: A plain-language framework for reading a government solicitation so you can identify the requirement, instructions, evaluation factors, deadlines, and contract terms that control your response.

sections.heading: Read the solicitation as a set of instructions, not a brochure
paragraphs: A government solicitation is designed to communicate a purchasing requirement and the rules for competing. The most important information may be spread across the main notice, attachments, clauses, amendments, exhibits, pricing schedules, statements of work, and proposal instructions.

For federal negotiated acquisitions, FAR 15.203 says a competitive request for proposals must describe the government's requirement, anticipated contract terms and conditions, the information required in the proposal, and the evaluation factors and their relative importance.

sections.heading: Identify the controlling dates and submission method
paragraphs: Before studying the opportunity in depth, identify the response deadline, time zone, submission location or portal, question deadline, site-visit or conference requirements, and any amendment acknowledgments. A technically strong proposal can still fail if it is submitted late or does not follow mandatory delivery instructions.
Check for amendments each time you return to the opportunity. An amendment can change dates, requirements, quantities, forms, or answers to vendor questions.

sections.heading: Separate the requirement from the response instructions
paragraphs: The scope tells you what the buyer needs. The proposal instructions tell you what evidence and format the buyer expects from you. Treat those as separate questions: Can we perform the requirement, and can we submit a compliant response by the deadline?
bullets: Scope or statement of work: what must be delivered or performed.
Qualifications: licenses, experience, personnel, certifications, clearances, or other prerequisites.
Proposal instructions: required volumes, forms, page limits, pricing formats, signatures, and attachments.
Evaluation factors: what the buyer says it will consider when comparing offers.
Contract terms: performance obligations, payment provisions, insurance, reporting, compliance, and other conditions.
Amendments: later changes that may modify the original solicitation.

sections.heading: Build a compliance checklist from the solicitation itself
paragraphs: Do not rely on memory or a generic proposal template. Convert the solicitation into a checklist that traces each mandatory instruction to the part of the response that satisfies it.

FAR 15.304 requires factors affecting federal source-selection decisions and their relative importance to be stated clearly in the solicitation. That makes the evaluation section especially important when deciding what evidence and emphasis belong in a proposal.

sections.heading: Resolve uncertainty before committing to a response
paragraphs: If a requirement is ambiguous, use the solicitation's stated question process or contracting contact rather than guessing. Record assumptions, unanswered questions, and dependencies before the bid decision.
The goal of solicitation review is not simply to understand the topic. It is to determine what the buyer requires, what your business must prove, and what a compliant response will demand.
